introduction_markdown:
**Time allowed: three hours.** This paper contains six questions arranged in three sections: Section A - Physical and General Chemistry (questions 1 and 2); Section B - Inorganic Chemistry (questions 3 and 4); Section C - Organic Chemistry (questions 5 and 6).

Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. No marks will be awarded for answers without brief statements showing how the answers have been obtained. Calculators may be used.

**Useful data:** one atmosphere (1 atm) = 1 Pa = $1.01\times10^{5}$ N m$^{-2}$ (as printed); relative atomic masses (RAM): C = 12.0, S = 32.0, O = 16.0, H = 1.0; molar gas volume at stp = 22400 cm$^3$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Name two close packed structures, giving an example of each. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Hexagonal close packing (hcp)**: layers repeat in the pattern **ABAB...** Examples: magnesium, zinc (also cadmium, titanium).
2. **Cubic close packing (ccp), i.e. face-centred cubic (fcc)**: layers repeat in the pattern **ABCABC...** Examples: copper, aluminium, silver, gold.

In both structures each atom is surrounded by **12 nearest neighbours** (co-ordination number 12) and about 74 % of the space is occupied by atoms.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the following equations and enthalpy changes in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

i. $\mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{SO_2(g)}$ $\Delta H_1 = -296.1$

ii. $\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)}$ $\Delta H_2 = -393.5$

iii. $\mathrm{CS_2(l)} + 3\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{SO_2(g)}$ $\Delta H_3 = -107.2$

Calculate the enthalpy of formation of carbon disulphide, $\mathrm{CS_2}$.

$\mathrm{C(s)} + 2\mathrm{S(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CS_2(s)}$ *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Apply Hess's law. The target equation (formation of $\mathrm{CS_2}$ from its elements) is obtained by taking equation ii, adding **2 x equation i**, and **reversing equation iii**:

$$\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2(g)} \quad \Delta H_2$$

$$2\mathrm{S(s)} + 2\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} \quad 2\Delta H_1$$

$$\mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CS_2(l)} + 3\mathrm{O_2(g)} \quad -\Delta H_3$$

Adding: $\mathrm{C(s)} + 2\mathrm{S(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CS_2(l)}$ (the $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ cancel).

$$\Delta H_f = \Delta H_2 + 2\Delta H_1 - \Delta H_3 = -393.5 + 2(-296.1) - (-107.2)$$

$$\Delta H_f = -393.5 - 592.2 + 107.2 = -878.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$$

**Answer: $\Delta H_f(\mathrm{CS_2}) = -878.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ with the data as printed.**

*Note on the data:* the printed $\Delta H_3 = -107.2\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ looks like a misprint (a digit lost): the tabulated enthalpy of combustion of carbon disulphide is about $-1075\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and its enthalpy of formation is positive, about $+88\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. With $\Delta H_3 = -1072.2$ the same method gives $+86.5\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. The working above follows the data printed in the paper.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Peroxodisulphate ions react with iodide ions according to the equation:

$\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{I^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{I_2} + 2\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ (all aqueous)

The following data was obtained for a series of mixtures:

| Experiment | $[\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}(aq)}]$ / $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ | $[\mathrm{I^-(aq)}]$ / $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ | Initial rate of reaction in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.038 | 0.030 | $7.0\times10^{-6}$ |
| 2 | 0.076 | 0.030 | $14.0\times10^{-6}$ |
| 3 | 0.076 | 0.060 | $28.0\times10^{-6}$ |

(i) What is the order of the reaction with respect to:

A: $\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}}$ ions.

B: Iodide ions.

(ii) Write the rate expression for the reaction.

(iii) Calculate the value of the rate constant stating the units. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Compare experiments in which only one concentration changes.

- **A:** experiments 1 and 2: $[\mathrm{I^-}]$ is constant ($0.030$) and $[\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}}]$ doubles ($0.038 \to 0.076$); the rate doubles ($7.0\times10^{-6} \to 14.0\times10^{-6}$). So the rate is proportional to $[\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}}]^1$: the reaction is **first order** with respect to peroxodisulphate ions.
- **B:** experiments 2 and 3: $[\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}}]$ is constant ($0.076$) and $[\mathrm{I^-}]$ doubles ($0.030 \to 0.060$); the rate doubles ($14.0\times10^{-6} \to 28.0\times10^{-6}$). The reaction is **first order** with respect to iodide ions.

**(ii)** $$\text{rate} = k\,[\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}}]\,[\mathrm{I^-}]$$ (overall second order).

**(iii)** From experiment 1: $k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}}][\mathrm{I^-}]} = \dfrac{7.0\times10^{-6}}{0.038 \times 0.030} = 6.14\times10^{-3}$.

Units: $\dfrac{\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}\,s^{-1}}}{(\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})^2} = \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

$$k = 6.14\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$$

Check with experiments 2 and 3: $\dfrac{14.0\times10^{-6}}{0.076\times0.030} = 6.14\times10^{-3}$ and $\dfrac{28.0\times10^{-6}}{0.076\times0.060} = 6.14\times10^{-3}$: the same value.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Propanoic acid, ($\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}$) is a weak acid with an acid dissociation constant $K_a$ of $1.22\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

(i) What is a weak acid?

(ii) Calculate the pH of a 0.2 M $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}$ solution. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A weak acid is an acid that is only **partially (slightly) dissociated** in aqueous solution, so the equilibrium $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^{-}} + \mathrm{H^{+}}$ lies far to the left and few $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions are produced.

**(ii)** $K_a = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^-}]}{[\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}]}$. Since the acid is the only source of ions, $[\mathrm{H^+}] = [\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^-}]$, and because dissociation is very small, $[\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}] \approx 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

$$[\mathrm{H^+}]^2 = K_a \times c = 1.22\times10^{-5} \times 0.2 = 2.44\times10^{-6}$$

$$[\mathrm{H^+}] = 1.56\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$$

$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.56\times10^{-3}) = 2.81$$

(The approximation is justified: only $\dfrac{1.56\times10^{-3}}{0.2} = 0.8\ \%$ of the acid is dissociated. Solving the quadratic exactly also gives pH = 2.81.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
A mixture of sodium propanoate ($\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COONa}$) and $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}$ acid acts as a buffer solution.

(i) What is a buffer solution?

(ii) Write equations to show what happens when a small amount of hydrochloric acid solution is added to the buffer. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A buffer solution is a solution that **resists changes in pH** when small amounts of acid or alkali (or a moderate dilution) are added. A weak acid together with its salt (a large reservoir of both $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}$ and $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^{-}}$) is an acidic buffer.

**(ii)** The propanoate ion (from the salt) removes the added $\mathrm{H^+}$ ions:

$\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COO^{-}} + \mathrm{H^{+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH}$

or, in full, $\mathrm{CH_3CH_2COONa} + \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2COOH} + \mathrm{NaCl}$

The added $\mathrm{H^+}$ is converted into the weak acid, so $[\mathrm{H^+}]$ and the pH change only very slightly (the ratio $[\mathrm{salt}]/[\mathrm{acid}]$ hardly changes).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Consider the following reaction in equilibrium at $350^\circ$C:

$\mathrm{CO(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3OH(l)}$ $\Delta H = +91\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

(i) State the equilibrium law.

(ii) What is the effect on the equilibrium position if the temperature of the system is increased?

Explain. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** *Equilibrium law:* at constant temperature, when a reversible reaction is at equilibrium, the product of the equilibrium concentrations (or partial pressures) of the products, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, divided by the same product for the reactants, is a constant, $K$.

For this reaction, methanol is a pure liquid (its concentration is constant and omitted):

$$K_p = \frac{1}{p_{\mathrm{CO}}\;p_{\mathrm{H_2}}^{2}}$$

**(ii)** The forward reaction is **endothermic** ($\Delta H = +91\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ as printed). By Le Chatelier's principle, when the temperature is raised the system opposes the change by absorbing heat, i.e. by favouring the endothermic (forward) reaction. The equilibrium position therefore **shifts to the right**, more methanol is formed and the value of $K$ increases.
